articles.title: Scientists shrink Archimedes’ screw to the size of a single molecule
articles.summary: Scientists have built a groundbreaking molecular motor that spins in either direction using electricity, inspired by a machine invented more than 2,000 years ago. Even more remarkably, its rotation can boost electrical conductivity by up to 100 times, potentially transforming the future of molecular electronics.
articles.content:
Scientists have developed a remarkable new molecular motor that spins when electricity passes through it. Inspired by an ancient invention, the tiny machine can even reverse its direction when the electrical voltage is switched. The achievement marks an important step toward creating working machines at the smallest possible scale.

Molecular machines are widely seen as a promising next frontier in miniaturization. Nature already provides examples inside living cells, where molecular motors use energy to produce movement. Researchers have spent decades trying to recreate these remarkable biological systems artificially, and progress in this field was recognized with the 2016 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

An Ancient Invention Inspires a Molecular Motor

Scientists first developed molecular motors powered directly by electricity in 2011. However, those earlier designs operated on surfaces and relied on the tip of a scanning tunneling microscope to drive their movement.

The new motor takes a different approach, borrowing its basic design from the Archimedes screw, one of the oldest machines in recorded history. Traditionally used to move water uphill, this simple device relies on a rotating spiral to transport material.

Researchers adapted that principle to the molecular scale. Instead of moving water, their design allows electrons to travel through a spiral-shaped molecule, causing it to rotate as electrical current passes through.

A Tiny Molecular Screw Suspended Between Gold Tips

The motor's central component is a specially designed spiral molecule created by the research group of Prof. Michael Pittelkow at the University of Copenhagen. Measuring only a few millionths of a millimeter, the molecule can attach to gold surfaces through sulfur atoms.

At the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel, researchers led by Prof. Oren Tal and Dr. Anil Kumar Singh positioned individual molecules between two gold tips sharpened to atomic dimensions. By carefully changing the separation between these electrodes, the team could stretch or compress the molecular screw.

When the scientists applied an electrical voltage, measurements revealed that the molecule began rotating. Even more importantly, they could reverse its direction simply by changing the voltage's polarity.

This represents the first demonstration of a molecular motor that is driven by electrical current, firmly connected to two metal electrodes, and capable of rotating in a controllable direction.

How Electricity Makes a Single Molecule Spin

The driving force comes directly from electrons traveling through the spiral molecule. As they move, they transfer angular momentum to the molecular structure, producing rotation in much the same way that moving air turns a wind turbine.

The spiral's shape determines how it responds to this flow, similar to the difference between screws with right- or left-handed threads. Once the applied voltage exceeds a certain threshold, the movement becomes continuous rotation.

But the experiments revealed another intriguing effect. The rotating molecule conducted electricity much more efficiently than it did when stationary, raising an important question about what was happening inside the tiny machine.

Scientists Discover a Surprising 100-Fold Electrical Effect

To investigate this unexpected behavior, Prof. Dr. Fabian Pauly and his PhD students Léon Martin and Yuta Ito, working at the Chair of Theoretical Physics I at the University of Augsburg, used quantum mechanical simulations on the LiCCA supercomputer.

Their calculations revealed a close relationship between the molecule's rotation and its ability to carry electrical current. Conductivity changes dramatically depending on the angle of the molecule, increasing by as much as two orders of magnitude, or 100 times, during rotation.

The reason turned out to be particularly surprising. Some of the molecular positions that allow electricity to pass most easily are also positions that the molecule naturally avoids when it is not moving. Rotation makes those highly conductive arrangements accessible.

"The surprising thing is that it is precisely the positions that the molecule avoids when at rest that conduct electricity best. It is only the rotation that makes these positions accessible," explains Léon Martin.

The finding demonstrates that molecular motion does more than simply consume electrical energy. The movement itself can strongly influence how electricity flows through the machine.

International Collaboration Solves the Mystery

The researchers then worked with theoretical physicists Per Hedegård of the Niels Bohr Institute in Copenhagen and Jing-Tao Lü of Huazhong University of Science and Technology in Wuhan.

Using the simulation results, the scientists developed a simplified theoretical model that successfully recreated both the rotation observed in the experiments and the accompanying increase in electrical current.

This combination of experimental measurements and theoretical calculations was essential to understanding the mechanism. Although researchers could measure the current passing through the molecule, they needed simulations to determine what was happening at such an extraordinarily small scale.

"In the experiment, you only see the current. Our calculations allow us to glimpse what is happening inside the nanocontact. It was only through close collaboration between experiment and theory across several countries that the mystery of the current increase could be solved," says Yuta Ito, a PhD student originally from Japan.

A New Frontier for Molecular Electronics

The achievement could eventually contribute to the development of molecular electronic components and technologies involving spintronics, which uses properties of electrons beyond their electrical charge. It may also offer possibilities for microfluidic systems, which manipulate extremely small quantities of fluids.

Beyond these potential applications, the motor provides scientists with a new way to investigate physical processes at the atomic scale. Its ability to convert electricity into controlled rotation, while allowing that rotation to influence electrical current, introduces a new principle for designing extraordinarily small machines.

"We have shown that an electric current can be used to generate a directed rotation and that this rotation, in turn, controls the current. This is a new operating principle for machines at the very limits of miniaturization," explains Pauly.

The work at the University of Augsburg received funding from the German Research Foundation (DFG) through Collaborative Research Center (SFB) 1585 (project number 492723217). The computational research was conducted using the University of Augsburg's LiCCA supercomputer (DFG project number 499211671).

Additional support for the collaborating institutions came from the European Research Council (ERC, Horizon 2020, Grant 864008), the Israel Science Foundation (2129/23), the Minerva Foundation, the Villum Foundation, the Novo Nordisk Foundation, the Independent Research Fund Denmark (DFF), the National Key Research and Development Program of China, and the National Natural Science Foundation of China.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific breakthrough in molecular motors, demonstrating a controllable molecular machine powered by electricity that can rotate and enhance electrical conductivity by 100 times. This advancement has broad implications for the future of molecular electronics and miniaturized machines, representing a meaningful step forward in technology with potential large-scale benefits.
articles.personality_title: Scientists create a tiny molecular motor that spins and boosts electricity
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientists have been working for years to build tiny machines called molecular motors. These machines are inspired by natural motors inside living cells and aim to work at an incredibly small scale, even at the level of single molecules.

**What happened** – A team of researchers created a new molecular motor based on the ancient Archimedes screw, which normally moves water uphill. This motor is a spiral-shaped molecule so small it’s only a few millionths of a millimeter long. When electricity passes through it, the molecule spins, and scientists can even reverse its spinning direction by changing the electrical voltage. The motor was tested by placing it between two gold tips and measuring its rotation and electrical behavior.

**Impact** – This motor does more than just spin. When it rotates, it makes electricity flow through it up to 100 times better than when it is still. This surprising discovery means the movement of the molecule directly helps electricity travel more easily. It is the first time a molecular motor has been shown to both spin controllably and improve electrical flow while connected to metal electrodes. This finding opens new possibilities for making tiny electronic devices and machines.

**What's next step** – Researchers will continue exploring how this motor and others like it can be used to build molecular electronic parts, devices that rely on electron properties called spintronics, and tiny systems that control fluids. They will also use this motor to better understand how electricity and motion interact at the smallest scale, helping design even smarter, smaller machines.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Scientists have built a tiny molecular motor that spins with electricity, can reverse direction, and boosts electrical flow by 100 times, offering new tools for future nanotechnology.
articles.personality_title_fr: Des scientifiques créent un moteur moléculaire minuscule qui tourne et améliore l’électricité
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Depuis des années, des scientifiques cherchent à construire de minuscules machines appelées moteurs moléculaires. Ces moteurs s’inspirent des moteurs naturels présents dans les cellules vivantes et ont pour but de fonctionner à une échelle incroyablement petite, jusqu’au niveau d’une seule molécule.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Une équipe de chercheurs a créé un nouveau moteur moléculaire basé sur la vis d’Archimède, une invention ancienne qui sert normalement à déplacer de l’eau en hauteur. Ce moteur est une molécule en spirale si petite qu’elle mesure seulement quelques millionièmes de millimètre. Lorsque de l’électricité la traverse, la molécule tourne, et les scientifiques peuvent même inverser le sens de cette rotation en changeant la tension électrique. Le moteur a été testé en le plaçant entre deux pointes d’or et en mesurant sa rotation et son comportement électrique.

**Impact** – Ce moteur ne se contente pas de tourner. Lorsqu’il tourne, il fait circuler l’électricité jusqu’à 100 fois mieux que lorsqu’il est immobile. Cette découverte surprenante signifie que le mouvement de la molécule aide directement l’électricité à mieux passer. C’est la première fois qu’un moteur moléculaire peut tourner de façon contrôlée et améliorer le passage du courant tout en étant connecté à des électrodes métalliques. Cette avancée ouvre de nouvelles possibilités pour fabriquer de minuscules appareils électroniques et machines.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs vont continuer à étudier comment ce moteur et d’autres similaires peuvent être utilisés pour construire des composants électroniques moléculaires, des dispositifs utilisant les propriétés des électrons appelés spintroniques, et des systèmes microscopiques contrôlant des fluides. Ils utiliseront aussi ce moteur pour mieux comprendre comment l’électricité et le mouvement interagissent à la plus petite échelle, afin de concevoir des machines encore plus petites et intelligentes.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Des scientifiques ont construit un moteur moléculaire minuscule qui tourne grâce à l’électricité, peut inverser sa direction et augmente le passage du courant par 100, offrant de nouveaux outils pour la nanotechnologie.
articles.personality_title_es: Científicos crean un motor molecular diminuto que gira y aumenta la electricidad
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Durante años, los científicos han intentado construir pequeñas máquinas llamadas motores moleculares. Estos motores están inspirados en motores naturales dentro de las células vivas y buscan funcionar a una escala increíblemente pequeña, hasta el nivel de una sola molécula.

**Qué pasó** – Un equipo de investigadores creó un nuevo motor molecular basado en el tornillo de Arquímedes, una máquina antigua que normalmente mueve agua hacia arriba. Este motor es una molécula en forma de espiral tan pequeña que mide solo unos pocos millonésimos de milímetro. Cuando pasa electricidad a través de ella, la molécula gira, y los científicos pueden incluso invertir la dirección del giro cambiando el voltaje eléctrico. El motor se probó colocándolo entre dos puntas de oro y midiendo su rotación y comportamiento eléctrico.

**Impacto** – Este motor hace más que girar. Cuando gira, permite que la electricidad fluya hasta 100 veces mejor que cuando está quieto. Este descubrimiento sorprendente significa que el movimiento de la molécula ayuda directamente a que la electricidad pase más fácilmente. Es la primera vez que un motor molecular puede girar de manera controlada y mejorar el flujo eléctrico mientras está conectado a electrodos metálicos. Este hallazgo abre nuevas posibilidades para fabricar dispositivos electrónicos y máquinas muy pequeñas.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores seguirán explorando cómo este motor y otros similares pueden usarse para construir componentes electrónicos moleculares, dispositivos que utilizan propiedades de los electrones llamadas espintrónica, y sistemas diminutos que controlan fluidos. También usarán este motor para entender mejor cómo interactúan la electricidad y el movimiento a la escala más pequeña, ayudando a diseñar máquinas aún más pequeñas e inteligentes.

**Resumen en una frase** – Científicos han creado un motor molecular diminuto que gira con electricidad, puede invertir su dirección y aumenta el flujo eléctrico hasta 100 veces, ofreciendo nuevas herramientas para la nanotecnología.

articles.title: How the US mid-term elections could shake up science
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 29 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03479-0A Democratic victory in Congress could halt the Trump administration’s controversial grant-review plan and curb some of its funding actions.
articles.content:
The upcoming US mid-term elections could change which political party controls Congress, which meets in the US Capitol building in Washington DC.Credit: Finn Gomez/Getty

As tens of millions of voters head to the polls on 3 November to cast ballots in the US mid-term elections, a political shake-up could be coming to Washington DC — with substantial consequences for the country’s scientific landscape.

Republicans currently hold more seats than do Democrats in both chambers of the US Congress, which has given the party and administration of President Donald Trump unified control of the federal government. But polling data favour Democrats to win back the House of Representatives and suggest that they have a chance of taking control of the Senate, too.

Since Trump took office last year, his administration has terminated thousands of research grants, slashed the federal scientific workforce and sought unprecedented political oversight of science agencies such as the US National Institutes of Health (NIH) and the US National Science Foundation (NSF). Many researchers and science advocates hope that a new Congress will stand up to the Trump administration to protect science funding and investigate its actions. “The Republican Congress has basically ceded their role in oversight for the last almost two years,” says Shaughnessy Naughton, president of 314 Action, a political fundraising group in Washington DC, which recruits and backs Democratic scientists, engineers and health-care specialists running for office.

Funding fight

The Trump administration has requested deep cuts to federal science budgets for the past couple of years, asking for the NSF’s budget, for example, to be cut by more than 50% in fiscal years 2026 and 2027. Both Republican and Democratic members of Congress, which sets the federal budget, have staved off those cuts so far. But the budget for the 2027 fiscal year, which began on 1 October, has not yet been officially approved.

White House proposes vast overhaul of US science funding: what you need to know

Even if Democrats, who have been backing boosts in science spending, were to win control of both chambers of Congress, it could be difficult to push through any major funding increases, because the final budget bills must still be signed by Trump.

At a minimum, researchers and science advocates hope that Congress will continue to prevent big budget cuts. But keeping budgets steady on paper has not stopped the administration from squeezing research in practice. Without congressional approval, the White House has curbed spending in other ways — terminating active grants mid-cycle and refusing to distribute money that Congress had already approved, a controversial tactic known as impoundment.

Science advocates say they hope that a new Congress will assert its budgetary power, namely by pushing back on these actions. The NSF, for instance, closed the 2026 fiscal year on 30 September with some US$1.4 billion in unspent funds, leading to the lowest number of new research grants issued in decades. The agency said that it has two years by law to spend its approved budget.

The Government Accountability Office (GAO), the investigative arm of Congress that has the ability to determine whether funds have been impounded, has rarely pursued action over violations, says Matt Dull, a specialist in government oversight at Virginia Tech, in Blacksburg, but the mid-terms could change the situation.

Controversial White House plan to overhaul US science funding faces Senate opposition

Another way that Congress could push back against the Trump administration’s reshaping of US science is to attach specific conditions to funding bills. For instance, because lawmakers haven’t yet agreed on the final budget for the 2027 fiscal year, they passed a ‘stopgap’ bill that funds the government only up to 11 December. The bill contains a section that temporarily blocks a White House plan to overhaul US science.

That plan is controversial: it would, for instance, put political appointees in charge of federal grant review and allow them to override the decisions of scientist peer reviewers. Giving control of grants to political appointees would threaten biomedical progress globally, says Ellie Dehoney, senior vice-president of policy and advocacy at Research!America, a non-profit organization in Arlington, Virginia. The White House Office of Management and Budget (OMB), which created the plan, said it did so to improve transparency, accountability and oversight of federal funds.

Rosa DeLauro, a Democratic representative from Connecticut, issued a statement last month saying that she was confident that Congress would continue blocking the OMB plan in future spending bills.

Increased oversight

Although Congress does not run US science agencies, it has oversight powers, which include launching investigations into agency actions. Most of these powers are reserved for the party in control of Congress, and Democrats have pledged to use them if they win big in the mid-terms.

‘Science needs defending’: record number of researchers run for office in US mid-terms

“We will continue the work we have been doing over the past two years to hold the Trump administration accountable,” says Zoe Lofgren, the most senior Democrat on the House Science, Space and Technology (SST) Committee. “If we win, we’ll have more tools at our disposal to do exactly that.” Lofgren and her Democratic colleagues have sent numerous letters to agencies such as the NSF and the US Department of Energy asking about actions such as grant terminations but have received few answers. If Democrats take control, Lofgren, who represents a California district and could become head of the SST committee, would have the ability to issue subpoenas, which can be used to compel administrators to testify in front of Congress.
articles.reasoning: The article discusses the potential positive impact of the US mid-term elections on science funding and oversight, highlighting how a Democratic victory could protect and possibly increase federal science budgets, halt controversial political interference in grant reviews, and strengthen congressional oversight. This has broad significance for the scientific community and society at large, as it could preserve and enhance scientific research funding and integrity.
articles.personality_title: US mid-term elections could protect and boost science funding
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – In the United States, mid-term elections happen every two years to decide which political party controls Congress. Right now, Republicans hold the majority, but Democrats may win more seats in the upcoming vote on November 3, 2026. This could affect how science is funded and overseen in the country.

**What happened** – The Trump administration has cut many research grants, reduced science jobs, and tried to put political leaders in charge of reviewing scientific research funding. If Democrats win control of the House of Representatives and possibly the Senate, they could stop these changes. Democrats want to protect science budgets and investigate the administration’s actions.

**Impact** – This matters because the government controls most funding for scientific research in the US. The Trump administration proposed big budget cuts and has sometimes stopped spending money that Congress already approved. A Democratic Congress could prevent these cuts, keep funding steady, and stop political interference in how grants are given. This would help scientists continue their work without unfair obstacles.

**What's next step** – After the elections, if Democrats gain power, they may pass laws to block the White House’s plan to put political appointees in charge of grant decisions. They could also use their power to investigate and demand answers from science agencies. For now, a temporary government funding bill stops the White House plan until December 11, 2026. The final budget for 2027 still needs approval.

**One-sentence takeaway** – The US mid-term elections could lead to stronger protection and support for scientific research by changing who controls Congress and how science funding is managed.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les élections de mi-mandat aux États-Unis pourraient protéger et renforcer le financement de la science
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Aux États-Unis, les élections de mi-mandat ont lieu tous les deux ans pour décider quel parti politique contrôle le Congrès. Actuellement, les Républicains ont la majorité, mais les Démocrates pourraient gagner plus de sièges lors du vote du 3 novembre 2026. Cela pourrait influencer le financement et la supervision de la science dans le pays.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – L’administration Trump a réduit de nombreuses subventions de recherche, diminué les emplois scientifiques et tenté de placer des responsables politiques à la tête de l’évaluation des financements scientifiques. Si les Démocrates prennent le contrôle de la Chambre des représentants et peut-être du Sénat, ils pourraient stopper ces changements. Ils souhaitent protéger les budgets scientifiques et enquêter sur les actions de l’administration.

**Impact** – Cela est important car le gouvernement contrôle la plupart des financements pour la recherche scientifique aux États-Unis. L’administration Trump a proposé de fortes coupures budgétaires et a parfois bloqué l’utilisation de fonds déjà approuvés par le Congrès. Un Congrès démocrate pourrait empêcher ces réductions, maintenir le financement stable et stopper les interférences politiques dans l’attribution des subventions. Cela aiderait les scientifiques à poursuivre leur travail sans obstacles injustes.

**Prochaine étape** – Après les élections, si les Démocrates prennent le pouvoir, ils pourraient adopter des lois pour bloquer le plan de la Maison-Blanche visant à placer des responsables politiques en charge des décisions sur les subventions. Ils pourraient aussi utiliser leur pouvoir pour enquêter et obtenir des réponses des agences scientifiques. Pour l’instant, un projet de loi provisoire bloque ce plan de la Maison-Blanche jusqu’au 11 décembre 2026. Le budget final pour 2027 doit encore être approuvé.

**Phrase clé** – Les élections de mi-mandat aux États-Unis pourraient renforcer la protection et le soutien à la recherche scientifique en modifiant le contrôle du Congrès et la gestion du financement de la science.
articles.personality_title_es: Las elecciones de medio término en EE. UU. podrían proteger y aumentar el financiamiento científico
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – En Estados Unidos, las elecciones de medio término se realizan cada dos años para decidir qué partido político controla el Congreso. Actualmente, los republicanos tienen la mayoría, pero los demócratas podrían ganar más escaños en las elecciones del 3 de noviembre de 2026. Esto podría afectar cómo se financia y supervisa la ciencia en el país.

**Qué pasó** – La administración Trump ha recortado muchas becas de investigación, reducido empleos científicos y tratado de poner a líderes políticos a cargo de revisar el financiamiento científico. Si los demócratas controlan la Cámara de Representantes y posiblemente el Senado, podrían detener estos cambios. Quieren proteger los presupuestos para la ciencia e investigar las acciones del gobierno.

**Impacto** – Esto es importante porque el gobierno controla la mayoría del dinero para la investigación científica en EE. UU. La administración Trump propuso grandes recortes y a veces detuvo el gasto de fondos ya aprobados por el Congreso. Un Congreso demócrata podría evitar estos recortes, mantener el financiamiento estable y frenar la interferencia política en la entrega de becas. Esto ayudaría a los científicos a continuar su trabajo sin obstáculos injustos.

**Próximo paso** – Después de las elecciones, si los demócratas ganan poder, podrían aprobar leyes para bloquear el plan de la Casa Blanca que pone a políticos a cargo de las decisiones sobre becas. También podrían usar su poder para investigar y obtener respuestas de las agencias científicas. Por ahora, una ley temporal detiene el plan de la Casa Blanca hasta el 11 de diciembre de 2026. El presupuesto final para 2027 aún debe aprobarse.

**Frase clave** – Las elecciones de medio término en EE. UU. podrían fortalecer la protección y el apoyo a la investigación científica al cambiar quién controla el Congreso y cómo se maneja el financiamiento de la ciencia.
